title: Human‐induced landscape of fear promotes coexistence in equids, facilitating the successful reintroduction of Przewalski's horses in the Gobi Desert
content:
Conceptual figure illustrating the main findings from Cao et al. (2025). In intact ecosystems (a), Przewalski's horses and Asiatic wild asses use the same water sources with some temporal partitioning (Przewalski's horses drink mostly during the day whereas Asiatic wild asses drink mostly at night). However, Asiatic wild asses can come in large herds (>100 individuals) and deplete the water at night, which prevents Przewalski's horses to use the water point until the next rain. In areas where humans are present (b), Asiatic wild asses avoid proximity to human infrastructures and hence do not drink from water points close to human infrastructures, which allows Przewalski's horses to continuously use these water points. The darkness of the blue colour for the water points indicates its filling level; the paler the blue, the more intense the depletion of the water.


Abstract

Research Highlight: Cao QL, Zhang Y, Songer M, Leimgruber P, Hu D, Li J, Wang C & Rubenstein DI (2025) Coexistence between Przewalski’s horse and Asiatic wild ass in the desert: the importance of people. Journal of Applied Ecology, https://doi.org/10.1111/1365-2664.70013.

The human imprint is complex and sometimes unpredictable and surprising. By instilling fear in some species, humans may provide refuges for other species. Using camera-trap data from 16 water points, Cao et al. originally showed how the coexistence of Przewalski’s horses and Asiatic wild asses in the Dzungarian Gobi is driven by the avoidance of water points near human infrastructures by Asiatic wild asses, which leaves some water points undepleted by the large herds of wild asses roaming in this region. Such finding is of high interest in a context of on-going efforts for the reintroduction of Przewalski’s horses in the Gobi Desert and of a context of a warmer and drier climate.
